overview.title: Chapter 15 opener: Language models and the Transformer
overview.main_topic: Opening of Chapter 15: generating text, English-to-Spanish translation, and the Transformer; the start of section 15.1 contrasts text classification with text generation.
overview.central_idea: Chapter 14 only had to map text to one number (or N numbers); Chapter 15 tackles problems where the output is itself text, which leads to language models, sequence-to-sequence translation and the Transformer.
overview.importance: This chapter introduces the Transformer, the architecture behind products like ChatGPT, and the language-model framing p(token | past tokens) that every generative text model in the rest of the book relies on.
learning_objectives: Know the three goals of the chapter: text generation, English-to-Spanish translation, and the Transformer architecture.
Explain why text classification is a 'uniquely simple' output problem compared with generating text.
Place section 15.1 (the language model) as the first step toward seq2seq and Transformers.

summary:
This is the **opening page of Chapter 15, *Language models and the Transformer***. The "This chapter covers" box lists three goals:

- **How to generate text with a deep learning model.** Section 15.1 builds a character-level Shakespeare language model (p.446-452).
- **Training a model to translate from English to Spanish.** Section 15.2 frames translation as sequence-to-sequence learning, first with RNNs (p.452-460).
- **The Transformer, a powerful architecture for text modeling problems.** Section 15.3 covers dot-product attention, encoder and decoder blocks, and positional embeddings (p.461-477). Section 15.4 then fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer encoder on IMDb (p.478-484), and section 15.5 asks what makes the Transformer effective (p.485).

The introductory paragraph says the chapter builds on Chapter 14's preprocessing basics to tackle "more involved language problems such as machine translation," and to build intuition for the Transformer, which "powers products like ChatGPT."

Section **15.1 The language model** begins at the bottom of the page. Chapter 14 converted text to numbers to classify reviews, but classification is "a uniquely simple problem": the output is a single float for binary classification, or at worst N numbers for N-way classification. The next page (p.446) shows why generating text is harder. The space of possible output sequences is astronomically large, so the practical approach is a model that predicts one token at a time, $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a roadmap. The pretraining idea from the end of Chapter 14 (p.444) reappears here at scale, since language modeling is the unsupervised task that Transformers are pretrained on.

paragraphs.excerpt: With the basics of text preprocessing and modeling covered in the previous chapter,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Chapter 15 moves on from Chapter 14's basics to harder language problems such as machine translation, and builds intuition for the Transformer, the model behind ChatGPT that has driven investment in NLP.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The tools from Chapter 14 (tokenizers, embeddings, sequence models) are reused, but the output side changes: the models must now produce text, not a label.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the Transformer as the chapter's main destination, with language modeling and translation as the problems that motivate it.

An attention-based sequence architecture introduced at the end of the 2010s (p.407), detailed in section 15.3.

paragraphs.excerpt: In the previous chapter, we learned how to convert text data to numeric inputs,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Chapter 14 turned text into numbers in order to classify reviews. Classification is a uniquely simple problem, since the output is one float (binary) or at most N numbers (N-way).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output space of a classifier is tiny and fixed. Generation has to choose among all possible token sequences, a space that grows exponentially with length. This contrast sets up the language-model idea on the next page.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing why classification is easy explains why a new modeling strategy is needed: predicting one token at a time and repeating.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book (spelled out on p.446): with a vocabulary of size $V$, there are $V^L$ sequences of length $L$. For $V=20{,}000$ and $L=4$ that is $1.6\times10^{17}$, far too many classes for a direct classifier.

terminology.meaning: Choosing among N classes; the model outputs N numbers, usually softmax probabilities.

connections: p.446: the next page computes 20,000^4 possible 4-word sequences and introduces p(token|past tokens).

concepts.name: Language model
concepts.definition: A model that predicts a probability distribution over the next token given the tokens seen so far, p(token | past tokens). Defined on p.446.
concepts.intuition: Autocomplete: guess the next word, append it, and guess again.
concepts.technical: Outputs a softmax over the vocabulary at each position. Repeated sampling generates sequences of any length while the output layer stays the size of the vocabulary.
concepts.significance: It turns an intractable sequence-output problem into a sequence of tractable classification problems, and it is the unsupervised pretraining task for modern LLMs.
concepts.example: The chapter's first model predicts the next character of Shakespeare text (section 15.1.1).
concepts.misconception: That a language model outputs whole sentences directly; it outputs one token's distribution at a time.

takeaways: Chapter 15 covers text generation, English-to-Spanish translation, and the Transformer.
Text classification is simple on the output side: one number, or N numbers.
Generating text requires a new framing, the language model, introduced in section 15.1.

questions.question: What are the three topics listed in the 'This chapter covers' box?
questions.answer: Generating text with a deep learning model; training a model to translate English to Spanish; the Transformer architecture for text modeling.
questions.explanation: Taken directly from the box on this page.

questions.question: Why do the authors call text classification 'a uniquely simple problem'?
questions.answer: Its output is tiny and fixed: one float for binary classification or N numbers for N-way classification. Generation has to produce a sequence chosen from an exponentially large space.
questions.explanation: Stated in section 15.1 on this page; the size of the generation space is quantified on p.446.

questions.question: Which product does the chapter introduction mention as being powered by the Transformer?
questions.explanation: The introduction says the Transformer 'powers products like ChatGPT'. The other products are not mentioned on this page.

questions.question: Before reading on: how would you design a model whose output is a sentence rather than a label? Write down your idea and compare it with p.446.
questions.answer: Open-ended; the book's answer is to predict one token at a time with p(token | past tokens) and repeat.
questions.explanation: Thinking about this first makes the language-model framing easier to absorb.

questions.question: How does the pretraining idea from the end of Chapter 14 relate to this chapter?
questions.answer: Language modeling is an unsupervised task on unlabeled text, the same kind of pretraining task Chapter 14 used CBOW for, but applied to whole models such as the Transformer encoder that is fine-tuned on IMDb in section 15.4.
questions.explanation: See p.444 for the pretraining summary and p.478-479 for pretraining a Transformer encoder.
